Experiment: (N.B. it would be useful to carry out this experiment, in exactly the same way, on cyclopentadecanolide and muscone, at the same time as the experiment with civettone, so that the results may be compared. Instructions are given accordingly.) Using a labelled beaker, prepare 50 g of any one completed fragrance experiment (see chapter 10, page 457 et seq), which you consider would be suitable as a personal fragrance. Label four, 50-ml beakers as follows: (a) 0.1% civettone in compound, (b) 0.1% cyclopentadecanolide in compound, (c) 0.1% muscone in compound and (d) control: compound only. Weigh into beaker (a) 0.01 g of civettone, and make up to 10.00 g with your perfume compound. Stir to dissolve the civettone. Similarly, make 0.1% solutions of cyclopentadecanolide and muscone in the respective beakers, and finally weigh 10 g of the perfume compound without any additions into beaker (d). N.B. Use a perfectly clean stirring rod for stirring each of the solutions. Close the beakers with cling film. Label four, 15-ml, or 1/2-ounce, amber glass bottles to correspond with the labels on the beakers, and transfer the solutions and control from the beakers to the respective bottles. Allow the solutions to stand, in a cool place, for one week, then chill them in a freezer at about OOC over 24 hours, to precipitate any matter insoluble at this temperature. In the meantime label four, 15-ml, or 1/2-oz, amber bottles as follows: Extrait (a) 10% compound containing 0.1% civettone, Extrait (b) 10% compound containing 0.1% cyclopentadecanolide, Extrait (c)

Applications: In fine perfumery, where its distinctive odour lends character and quality to fragrances such as Violet and Mimosa. Notes of Orris are fundamental to the bouquet of many successful extrait perfumes and toilet waters
Natural_Source: The finely comminuted rhizome of Iris pallida, peeled and dried for three years
Production: Steam distillation in equipment designed to accommodate a solid distillate
Chief_Constituents: Isomers of irone, myristic acid, furfural, aldehydes C9, C 10 non-2-en-1-al, linalool, geraniol No recommended restrictions
Experiment: As a 20% solution, with an accord of Rose, Jasmin and Orange Blossom. See experiments (pages 453, 448 and 452, respectively)
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.286

Appearance: Pale yellow to olive green, mobile liquid
Applications: For its lingering rosy notes in many perfume types in soap or household product perfumery, and for the isolation of geraniol
Natural_Source: Leaves of the grass, Cymbopogon motia
Chief_Constituents: Geraniol, geranyl acetate, 6-methylhept-5-en-2-one, farnesol, linalool, caryophyllene No recommended restrictions
Experiment: With Ylang-Ylang Oil No.3 Patchouli Oil
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.287

Appearance: Light to dark orange brown, slightly viscous liquid
Applications: For the varied and otherwise unobtainable effects to which this oil can give rise, usually in very small dosages, in combination with other materials. Frequently, in larger proportions, a fundamental note in Oriental-type perfumes.
Natural_Source: Dried and lightly fermented leaves of Pogostemon patchouli
Chief_Constituents: Norpatchoulenol, patchoulol, patchoulene, camphene, alpha- bulnesene, alpha-guaiene, caryophyllene, seychellene No recommended restrictions
Experiment: As a 20% solution, with any of the suggested creative experiments (pages 443 to 456) or with accords of these experiments, such as Lily-of-the-Valley (page 450), or Rose (page 453) with Jasmin (page 448)
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.287

Appearance: Colourless to pale yellow, somewhat viscous liquid
Applications: An excellent fixative of wide applications in Carnation and heavier florals, in Rose and Oriental fragrances
Natural_Source: The pathological oleoresin exuded from the Gunk of Myroxylon pereirae
Chief_Constituents: Benzyl benzoate, benzyl cinnamate, vanillin, cinnamyl alcohol, nerolidol, farnesol Recommended restriction: 2% in a perfume compound
Experiment: With a Carnation base (page 444) Petitgrain Oil, Bigarade
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.288

Appearance: Pale yellow to amber, mobile liquid
Applications: In Eaux de Cologne, as a replacement for the very much more costly Neroli Oil, in Neroli perfume bases and fragrances
Natural_Source: Leaves and green twigs of Citrus aurantium, var amara
Chief_Constituents: Linalool, linalyl acetate, geraniol, geranyl acetate, methyl anthranilate, limonenes No recommended restrictions
Experiment: With Bergamot Oil
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.288

Appearance: Pale to dark yellow, mobile liquid
Applications: Very widely used in soap perfumery, in Eaux de Cologne, floral and Oriental compositions
Natural_Source: Leaves and green twigs of cultivated trees of Citrus aurantium, var amara
Chief_Constituents: Linalool, linalyl acetate, geraniol, geranyl acetate, methyl anthranilate, limonenes No recommended restrictions
Experiment: With geranyl nitrile Pine Oil, Siberian
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.289

Appearance: Colourless to pale yellow, slightly viscous liquid
Applications: In perfumes for foam bath, shower gels and other bathtime preparations, also household products
Natural_Source: Needles and twigs of the tree, Abies sibirica
Chief_Constituents: Pinenes, myrcene, delta-3-carene, bornyl acetate, camphene, phellandrene, bisabolene Essential oils from the Pinus and Abies genera should be used only when they have a peroxide value of less than 10 millimoles of peroxide per litre, determined according to the Essential Oil Association method
Experiment: With iso-amyl salicylate
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.289

Applications: In fine perfumery and, in small dosages, as a 'naturaliser' of Rose and other floral notes in perfumes for high quality mass- market perfumes as, for example, floral, aldehydic Oriental and Chypre types
Natural_Source: Freshly picked flowers of Rosa centifolia
Production: Extraction of Rose de Mai Concrete with ethanol
Chief_Constituents: Geraniol, geranyl acetate, geranyl isobutyrate, phenylethyl acetate, citronellol, citronellyl acetate, phenylethyl alcohol, eugenol, linalool, nerol, rose oxides aldehydes C9 and CIO, beta-pinene, beta-farnesene No recommended restrictions
Experiment: As a 10% solution, (a) with a Jasmin base (page 448) and (b) with Sandalwood Oil, East Indian Rosemary Oil
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.290

Appearance: Colourless to pale yellow, mobile liquid
Applications: In Eaux de Cologne, Lavender and Oriental fragrances, also in fresh Pine, 'forest', Fougöre and Oriental perfumes for bathtime and household products
Natural_Source: Aerial parts of Rosmarinus officinalis
Chief_Constituents: Borneol, bornyl acetate, cineole, camphor, camphene, limonenes, alpha-terpineol, pinenes No recommended restrictions
Experiment: With linalyl acetate
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.290

Appearance: Pale yellow liquid, containing colourless, odourless, leafy crystals at cool temperatures. The product liquefies on a warm day, and solidifies to a crystalline mass on a cold day, the transition point being 21 oc for a genuine sample
Applications: A costly, but very cost-effective product, finding important, usually low-dosage, use in fine perfumery and in fragrances for mass-market products, to boost floral power and impart natural notes of Rose. Extremely versatile, usable in almost every type of perfume where it can be afforded
Natural_Source: Freshly gathered flowers of Rosa damascena
Chief_Constituents: Citronellol, citronellyl acetate, geraniol, nerol and neryl acetates, phenylethyl alcohol, eugenol, aldehyde C9, rose oxides, rose furan, nerol oxide, beta-damascone, beta- damascenone No recommended restrictions
Experiment: As a 10% solution, with a Rose base (page 453) Sandalwood Oil, East Indian
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.291

Appearance: Pale yellow to darker yellow, moderately viscous liquid
Applications: A superior fixative and blender for use, when affordable, in many perfume types, from florals to from aldehydics to Orientals. Only the cost of Sandalwood Oil, East Indian, restricts the use of this outstanding material
Natural_Source: The comminuted heartwood of mature, cultivated trees of Santalum album
Chief_Constituents: Alpha- and beta-santalols, alpha- and beta-santalenes, geraniol, citronellol, alpha-terpineol, para-methyl acetophenone, carvone No recommended restrictions
Experiment: With a balanced blend of Rose and Jasmin bases (pages 453 and 448, respectively)
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.291

Appearance: Pale yellow to brownish yellow, viscous liquid
Applications: As a fixative and blender, mainly for soap perfumes. Used also for the isolation of valerianol, from which nootkatone, used in perfumery for its Grapefruit-related note, is manufactured
Natural_Source: The comminuted heartwood of Amyris balsamifera
Chief_Constituents: Elemol, eudesmol, valerianol, agarofuran No recommended restrictions
Experiment: With iso-amyl salicylate, to evaluate the fixative power of this essential oil Styrax Oil
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.292

Appearance: Colourless to pale yellow, viscous liquid
Applications: In florals, such as Hyacinth, Lilac and Carnation
Natural_Source: The pathological oleoresin exuded from the trunk of the tree Liquidambar orientalis or Liquidambar styraciflua
Chief_Constituents: Styrene, cinnamyl alcohol, esters of cinnamyl alcohol, ethyl cinnamate No recommended restrictions
Experiment: With a Hyacinth base (page 447). Compare with the effect of the same proportion of Styrax Resinoid in the same base
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.292

Applications: As a fixative for floral compositions, such as Hyacinth, Lilac and Carnation
Natural_Source: The pathological oleoresin exuded from the trunk of the tree Liquidambar orientalis or Liquidambar styraciflua
Chief_Constituents: Styrene, cinnamyl alcohol, cinnamic acid, esters of cinnamyl alcohol and of cinnamic acid, vanillin, phenylpropyl alcohol, odourless resin Genuine gums and resins of Styrax should not be used as fragrance ingredients, but rather to use preparations free from allergens, eg, those resulting from neutralisation with aqueous alkali, followed by solvent extraction
Experiment: With a Hyacinth base (page 447). Compare with the effect of the same proportion of Styrax Oil in the same base Tagetes Oil
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.293

Applications: In small dosages, in the creation of Apple and other fruity fragrance effects for toilet preparations
Natural_Source: Aerial parts of Tagetes glandulifera—the 'Khaki Bush'
Chief_Constituents: linalool, cis-Tagetone, trans-tagetone, dihydrotagetone, ocimene No recommended restrictions
Experiment: As a 10% solution, with Bergamot Oil
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.293

Appearance: Colourless to pale yellow, mobile liquid
Applications: Usually in traces, for special effects in Chypre, and 'white flowers' perfume types
Natural_Source: Aerial parts of the herb, Artemisia dracunculus
Chief_Constituents: Estragole (methyl chavicol), limonenes, pinenes, sabinene, ocimene, methyl eugenol, elemicin No recommended restrictions
Experiment: As a 10% solution, with Lavender Oil Thyme Oil, Rectified (White Thyme Oil)
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.294

Applications: To impart fresh and 'medicated' notes to perfumes for toilet soaps; also, in small dosages, in Eaux de Cologne and, in traces, for freshening top notes
Natural_Source: Partially dried, aerial parts of the herb, Thymus vulgaris, and other species of Thymus
Chief_Constituents: Thymol, alpha-terpineol, camphor, borneol, carvacrol, myrcene No recommended restrictions
Experiment: With Bergamot Oil
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.294

Appearance: Colourless to pale yellow, viscous liquid
Applications: In floral perfumes, such as Honeysuckle, Hyacinth, Gardenia and Tuberose, and as a fixative
Natural_Source: Pathological oleoresin exuded from the trunk of the tree, Myroxylon toluifera
Production: Dry, vacuum distillation of the oleo-resin
Chief_Constituents: Benzyl cinnamate, benzyl benzoate, cinnamyl alcohol, cinnamic aldehyde
Experiment: With Musk T (Takasago) Tolu Balsam Resinoid
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.295

Appearance: Pale to dark brown, highly viscous liquid
Applications: As a fixative in floral, floriental, Chypre and Oriental-type perfume compositions, also an ingredient of perfume compounds for Eaux de Cologne and modern, masculine toilet waters
Natural_Source: Pathological oleo-resin exuded from the trunk of the tree, Myroxylon toluifera
Chief_Constituents: Cinnamyl alcohol, cinnamic aldehyde, ethyl benzoate, benzyl benzoate, cinnamyl benzoate, benzyl cinnamate, vanillin
Experiment: With an Orange Blossom base (page 452)
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.295

Appearance: Pale brown mass containing colourless crystals
Applications: In fine fragrance, as a fixative and contributory odour complex for Chypre, Tabac and Oriental-type compositions
Natural_Source: The dried, comminuted seeds ('beans') of Dipteryx odorata
Production: Extraction of Tonka Concrete with ethanol
Chief_Constituents: Coumarin No recommended restrictions
Experiment: As a 20% solution, with Lavender Oil Treemoss Absolute
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.296

Appearance: Green brown to brown, semi-solid mass
Applications: Largely in soap perfumery (if necessary as the decolorised absolute) as a fixative, and to supply the requisite 'mossy' notes in and related perfumes
Natural_Source: The lichens Pseudeverniafuffuracea and Usnea barbata
Production: Extraction of Treemoss Concrete with ethanol
Chief_Constituents: Methyl beta-orcinol carboxylate, olivetonide Recommended restriction of 3% in a fragrance compound
Experiment: With a 5% solution of coumarin in Lavender Oil, for comparison with the effect of Oakmoss Absolute in a parallel experiment
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.296

Applications: In fine fragrance, for sweet and heavy perfumes, such as Gardenia, Lilac and Plumeria, also in Oriental fragrances
Natural_Source: Freshly gathered flowers of Polyanthes tuberosa
Geographical_Source: Southern France, Morocco, Republic of China
Production: Extraction of Tuberose Concrete or pommade with ethanol
Chief_Constituents: Methyl benzoate, benzyl benzoate, methyl salicylate, methyl anthranilate, benzyl alcohol, alpha-terpineol, cineole, farnesol, macrocyclic lactones
Experiment: As a 10% solution, with Lyral (IFF) Turpentine Oil
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.297

Stability: Stable, but can cause discoloration in the presence of alkali or amines (anthranilates, indole etc)
Applications: In fine perfumery to impart sweetness, richness and depth to heavier florals and Oriental-type fragrances
Natural_Source: Cured fruits ('beans') of cultivated plants of the orchid Vanilla planifolia, Vanilla pompona and Vanilla tahitensis
Production: Solvent extraction of the dried fruits
Chief_Constituents: Vanillin, benzaldehyde, benzoic acid, salicylic aldehyde, 3,4- dihydroxy-benzaldehyde, 4-methoxybenzyl alcohol, ferulic acid No recommended restrictions
Experiment: As a 10% solution with anisyl acetate Vetivert Oil
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.298

Appearance: Light amber to dark brown, viscous liquid
Applications: Excellent fixative and superior woody note, used in Chypre, woody bases, Oriental-type perfumes and certain florals, such as Rose, Violet and Orchid
Natural_Source: Rootlets of Vetiveria zizanoides, soaked in water and chopped
Chief_Constituents: 'Vertiverol' (a mixture of sesquiterpene alcohols), alpha- and beta-vetivones, vetivenene, elemol, alpha-ylangene, khusimone No recommended restrictions
Experiment: With iso-amyl salicylate
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.298

Appearance: Dark green, viscous to mobile liquid
Applications: In very small dosages, for natural green effects in floral and almost any other type of perfume where this kind of nuance is required
Natural_Source: The leaves of the plant, Viola odorata
Production: Extraction of Violet Leaf Concrete with ethanol
Chief_Constituents: 2-trans-6-cis-nonadien-1-al, cis-hex-3-en-1-ol, trans-hex-2- en-l-ol, dodecan-l-ol, cis-hex-3-en-1-yl formate, benzyl alcohol No recommended restrictions
Experiment: As a 10% solution, with a Violet base (page 456)
Source: Curtis & Williams, An Introduction to Perfumery (1994) Ch 6 monograph, PDF p.299
